questions.statement: Which opening is the most formal way to begin the body of the email?
questions.context: A student must open a formal email to the principal to request a change.

options.text: I am writing to request an extension of the library deadline for our group project.
options.feedback: Correct. 'I am writing to...' states the purpose of the letter formally and tells the reader immediately why the message exists.

options.text: Hey, could you please maybe extend the deadline for our group project?
options.feedback: The greeting and the request are informal and hedged, which suits a message to a classmate rather than to the principal.

options.text: Just a quick note to say that we would be really grateful if the deadline could move.
options.feedback: 'Just a quick note' is conversational and 'really grateful' is too familiar for a formal request.

options.text: You need to extend our deadline because we have not finished the project yet.
options.feedback: This is a blunt instruction to the reader and it gives a reason the writer should present politely instead.

questions.explanation:
A formal letter opens by naming the purpose in a full clause such as I am writing to enquire about or I am writing to request.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence states the reason for a request correctly?
questions.context: A formal letter must make a polite request rather than a demand.

options.text: I would be grateful if you could approve our request, since the equipment is already booked for that date.
options.feedback: Correct. The reason explains the circumstances behind the request and is attached with 'since', which keeps the tone courteous.

options.text: Approve our request, because the equipment is already booked.
options.feedback: It opens with an imperative and gives the reason as an afterthought, which reads as an order.

options.text: You do not have to approve it, although the equipment is already booked for that date.
options.feedback: The condition is stated as optional and no request is actually made, so the sentence communicates nothing to act on.

options.text: Since the equipment is already booked, this is impossible for us to send to the office.
options.feedback: The sentence reports a problem instead of making a request, so the reader is left without an action to take.

questions.explanation:
A request is made politely with I would be grateful if or I would appreciate it if, and the reason for it follows a connector such as since or because.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is appropriate for ending a formal letter that asks for action?
questions.context: A student must end a formal letter that asks the reader to take an action.

options.text: I look forward to your reply. Thank you for your time and consideration.
options.feedback: Correct. It invites a response and closes with thanks, which are the two conventional moves at the end of a formal letter.

options.text: Bye! Let me know soon, please.
options.feedback: The sign-off is informal and the pressure to reply is placed on the reader rather than requested politely.

options.text: Yours, and that is all I needed to say about this matter.
options.feedback: The closing is curt and ungrateful, which is not the register a formal letter requires.

options.text: I hope you will not ignore this email, because I have already waited two weeks.
options.feedback: This is an accusation rather than a courtesy and undermines the polite request made earlier in the letter.

questions.explanation:
A formal letter ends by inviting a reply and thanking the reader, followed by a formal sign-off such as Yours faithfully.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is the best formal expression of regret for the delay?
questions.context: A student must apologise for a late reply in a formal email to a supplier.

options.text: I sincerely apologise for the delay in replying to your enquiry of 3 March.
options.feedback: Correct. 'I sincerely apologise' is a formal acknowledgement and the date identifies exactly which message is being referred to.

options.text: Sorry, the reply is late. I have been very busy and also the mail is slow.
options.feedback: It is too casual for a business message and the excuses put the blame outside the writer's control.

options.text: The reply is late, and in my opinion the office should have replied faster.
options.feedback: This criticises another party instead of accepting responsibility, so no apology is actually made.

options.text: Please accept that the reply was late, although it was not my fault.
options.feedback: 'Please accept' demands rather than apologises, and the denial of responsibility weakens the apology.

questions.explanation:
A formal apology uses I apologise or I am sorry for, accepts responsibility and names the specific matter, without excuses.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence states contact details correctly for a formal letter?
questions.context: A student must give contact details at the end of a formal application letter.

options.text: You can reach me at 787-555-0142 or at marina.torres@example.com.
options.feedback: Correct. It offers two complete channels and names the means of reaching the writer, which lets the reader respond without difficulty.

options.text: You can reach me at 787-555-0142 or maybe somewhere near my house.
options.feedback: The second option is not usable, so a reader who cannot call is left with no way to reply.

options.text: My phone and my mailbox are both the best ways to contact me.
options.feedback: The sentence describes the methods in general instead of giving the actual numbers and addresses needed.

options.text: Email me at example.com, and my telephone is on the letterhead of this paper.
options.feedback: The address is given backwards and the phone number is only stated to exist, not to be readable.

questions.explanation:
Contact details in a formal letter are written out in full, with at least one usable channel such as a full telephone number or a complete email address.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is appropriate in the body of a formal letter of enquiry?
questions.context: A student must decide which version of a sentence is appropriate for a formal letter of enquiry.

options.text: I am writing to enquire whether your office could send the annual report by post.
options.feedback: Correct. 'I am writing to enquire whether' is the standard formal opening for a letter that asks for information.

options.text: Send the annual report to my house as soon as you can, please.
options.feedback: The imperative gives an instruction rather than enquiring, which changes the purpose of the letter entirely.

options.text: I am writing to tell you what happened with the annual report last year.
options.feedback: This reports the past instead of asking about something, so the reader has no request to act on.

options.text: Just wondering if you might possibly post the report out at some point.
options.feedback: The chain of hedges sounds conversational and uncertain rather than formal and businesslike.

questions.explanation:
A letter of enquiry names the purpose with a formal formula such as I am writing to enquire about and then states the specific request in indirect terms.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which salutation is correct when the name of the person receiving the letter is unknown?
questions.context: A student must choose between two salutations for a formal letter to an unknown reader.

options.text: Dear Sir or Madam,
options.feedback: Correct. This is the conventional salutation when the recipient is not named, and it pairs with the closing Yours faithfully.

options.text: Hey you,
options.feedback: This greeting is conversational and would be inappropriate in any formal letter.

options.text: Hi everyone,
options.feedback: The plural greeting suggests a group chat and does not address a single professional reader.

options.text: My friend,
options.feedback: It implies personal familiarity that the writer has not established with the reader.

questions.explanation:
Dear Sir or Madam is the standard salutation for an unnamed recipient, and it requires the closing Yours faithfully rather than Yours sincerely.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sequence of parts is correct for a short formal email?
questions.context: A student must organise the three conventional parts of a formal email.

options.text: Purpose, details and request, closing thanks, then the sign-off.
options.feedback: Correct. The reader learns why the message exists, what is being asked, and how the writer closes, in that order.

options.text: Sign-off, purpose, closing thanks, then the details and the request.
options.feedback: Beginning with the sign-off removes the heading the reader needs before the rest makes sense.

options.text: Request, purpose, sign-off, then closing thanks and the details of the request.
options.feedback: The request appears before the purpose that would explain it, and the sign-off interrupts the body.

options.text: Details, closing thanks, purpose, then the request and finally the sign-off.
options.feedback: The reader meets the facts before knowing why they matter, which is the reverse of the expected order.

questions.explanation:
A short formal email states the purpose, gives the details with the request, thanks the reader and closes formally, in that order.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which detail is least necessary in a short formal letter?
questions.context: A student must decide what to leave out of a short formal letter.

options.text: A full description of the writer's weekend and the weather during the trip.
options.feedback: Correct. Nothing about a weekend or the weather affects the request, and a formal letter keeps only what the reader needs to act.

options.text: The date on which the writer is travelling.
options.feedback: The travel date determines whether the request can be met, so it is essential to the reader's decision.

options.text: The reference number of the booking being changed.
options.feedback: The reference lets the office find the file immediately and without a second letter.

options.text: The specific change the writer is asking for.
options.feedback: The precise request is the point of the letter, so it can never be left out.

questions.explanation:
A short formal letter keeps every detail the reader needs in order to act: dates, references and the exact request, and drops personal background.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which revision presents the same request in the register a formal email requires?
questions.context: A student's formal email repeats the same point three times and buries the request.

options.text: Replace the repeated plea with 'I would be grateful if you could confirm the room booking by Friday'.
options.feedback: Correct. The revision states the request once, in indirect form, and attaches a clear deadline.

options.text: Repeat the request at the beginning, in the middle and at the end so it cannot be missed.
options.feedback: Repetition in formal writing reads as padding rather than emphasis and buries the body of the email.

options.text: Add 'please' several times to every sentence so the tone becomes more formal.
options.feedback: Repeating please does not change the register, and several polite words in one sentence read oddly.

options.text: Remove the request entirely and describe the situation so the reader infers it.
options.feedback: With no explicit request the reader must guess what is wanted, which is the opposite of clear formal writing.

questions.explanation:
Formal writing is concise and indirect: one clearly stated request in a courteous form, not repetition or a string of intensifiers.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sign-off matches a letter addressed to a named person you know?
questions.context: A student must choose the correct closing for a letter addressed to a named colleague.

options.text: Yours sincerely,
options.feedback: Correct. Yours sincerely is used when the recipient is named, while an unnamed recipient requires Yours faithfully.

options.text: Yours faithfully,
options.feedback: This closing is for an unnamed recipient, so pairing it with a named addressee is a mismatch.

options.text: See you around,
options.feedback: The sign-off is conversational and does not close a formal letter.

options.text: Goodbye forever and ever,
options.feedback: The hyperbole is not a formal closing and would confuse rather than impress the reader.

questions.explanation:
The closing depends on the addressee: Yours sincerely for a named recipient, Yours faithfully for an unnamed one.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is the best way to explain a delay formally?
questions.context: A student must give a reason for a late reply in a formal email to a university office.

options.text: I was unable to submit the form earlier because the office was closed during the holiday period.
options.feedback: Correct. It states the reason in a neutral, verifiable way without complaining about the delay itself.

options.text: Your office is always closed at the worst moment and I could not do anything about it.
options.feedback: This assigns blame to the reader, which is inappropriate in a formal message to an office.

options.text: I was too busy with my own work to bother with the form.
options.feedback: The admission is candid but informal and puts the writer in a poor light in a formal letter.

options.text: The form is impossible for anyone to fill in, since the instructions are very confusing.
options.feedback: This criticises the document instead of explaining a specific personal obstacle, so it deflects rather than informs.

questions.explanation:
A formal explanation of a delay gives a neutral verifiable cause, states it without complaining and avoids blaming the reader.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence keeps the correct register in a complaint to a company?
questions.context: A student must write to a business about a faulty item and wants the tone to remain formal.

options.text: The kettle arrived damaged on 12 April, and I am writing to request a replacement under the guarantee.
options.feedback: Correct. It records the facts with a date and states the remedy formally, without either accusing or excusing the company.

options.text: Your useless kettle arrived broken and you people have no idea how to run a shop.
options.feedback: The insult and the familiar 'you people' belong to an argument, not to a formal complaint.

options.text: Kettle broken, delivery terrible, refund please, thanks a lot.
options.feedback: This telegraphic list omits dates and the grounds for the claim, so the company could not act on it.

options.text: I am writing to complain about the kettle, which is a product, and it was not as expected.
options.feedback: Calling the kettle a product and saying it was not as expected state no fault and ask for no remedy.

questions.explanation:
A formal complaint states what happened, when it happened and what remedy is requested, keeping anger out of the language.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence states the purpose of an attached document correctly?
questions.context: A student must attach information to a formal email without being abrupt.

options.text: Please find attached the completed form required for the sports permit.
options.feedback: Correct. It names what is attached, explains why it is needed and uses the conventional formula 'please find attached'.

options.text: Attached is the form, which you need, and you will need it soon.
options.feedback: The inverted sentence omits the purpose and repeats the need, which makes the instruction harder to follow.

options.text: I send you now the thing that is attached at the end of this message.
options.feedback: The wording is vague and informal and never states what the document is or what it is for.

options.text: You will not be able to do anything without the document, and it is attached.
options.feedback: The opening is a threat rather than an explanation and the sentence never names the document.

questions.explanation:
A formal email says what is attached and why it is needed, normally with the formula please find attached followed by the name of the document.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is the most appropriate closing for this type of formal email?
questions.context: A student must decide which closing sentence suits a formal email about a job application.

options.text: Thank you for considering my application, and I would be glad to provide any further information.
options.feedback: Correct. It thanks the reader, acknowledges the reader's decision and leaves the door open, all in measured formal language.

options.text: Hope you like my application because I worked really hard on it for weeks.
options.feedback: The first-person emphasis and the contraction belong to an informal message to a friend.

options.text: Send me an answer now, because I need to know as soon as possible.
options.feedback: This is a demand rather than a courteous close and applies pressure to the reader.

options.text: That is everything, although I might write again later with more details.
options.feedback: The hint at further messages leaves the reader unsure whether the application is complete or still open.

questions.explanation:
A professional closing thanks the reader, acknowledges the decision that is awaited and offers further help, without demanding or hinting.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence gives a formal recommendation supported by an observation?
questions.context: A student must recommend a colleague for a post in a formal recommendation letter.

options.text: She led the team that reorganised the archive, and the catalogue was complete three months ahead of schedule.
options.feedback: Correct. It names the specific contribution and an outcome with a timeframe, which is the kind of detail a reader can weigh.

options.text: She is a wonderful person and the best colleague anyone could ask for.
options.feedback: This is praise with no evidence, and a reader cannot judge a recommendation built only on adjectives.

options.text: She is very good at her job and she is also very good at other jobs.
options.feedback: The repeated vague claim restates the praise without adding a single fact about her work.

options.text: I have worked with her since I was at school, so I know her very well indeed.
options.feedback: This establishes familiarity but says nothing about the candidate's ability, which is what the letter must report.

questions.explanation:
A formal recommendation supports its judgement with a specific observation and an outcome, not with adjectives or with the writer's own closeness to the candidate.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence makes an indirect request that is appropriate for a formal email?
questions.context: A student must make an indirect request instead of a direct instruction in a formal email.

options.text: I would appreciate it if you could send me the signed form before the end of the week.
options.feedback: Correct. 'I would appreciate it if' is the standard indirect form, and the request is followed by a clear timeframe.

options.text: Send me the signed form before the end of the week without forgetting it.
options.feedback: This is a command with an added reproach, which is the wrong register for a formal email.

options.text: It would not be a bad idea if the signed form reached me before the end of the week.
options.feedback: The hedged suggestion is so weak that the reader may not recognise it as a request at all.

options.text: The signed form, which you will send me, is due before the end of the week.
options.feedback: The clause asserts the reader's future action instead of requesting it politely.

questions.explanation:
Formal requests are indirect, using I would appreciate it if or I would be grateful if you could, and they state the deadline plainly.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence avoids a pronoun whose referent is unclear?
questions.context: A student must choose the wording that avoids an ambiguous pronoun in a formal email.

options.text: The office will confirm your booking by email once the deposit has been paid.
options.feedback: Correct. Each clause names its own subject, so no reader has to guess who confirmed the booking or who paid the deposit.

options.text: They will confirm it once you have paid, and they usually do it quickly.
options.feedback: Both pronouns are ambiguous: they and it have no clear referent anywhere in the sentence.

options.text: It will be confirmed by them after it has been paid by you.
options.feedback: The passive stacking of it and them leaves the reader guessing which nouns were replaced.

options.text: That is confirmed by them when it is paid, as is normally done.
options.feedback: That and it refer to nothing that has been named, and as is normally done adds no content.

questions.explanation:
Formal writing avoids ambiguous pronouns because a letter may be read by several people; naming each subject keeps the reference clear.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is least appropriate in a short formal letter?
questions.context: A student must decide which sentence is least necessary in a short formal letter, given that the writer must remain clear and courteous.

options.text: Well, that is my idea anyway, so do whatever you want about it, whatever.
options.feedback: Correct. The repeated fillers and the casual dismissal of the matter are incompatible with the courtesy a formal letter requires.

options.text: I am writing to confirm the arrangements for the visit on 4 May.
options.feedback: This states the purpose precisely and belongs in the opening of such a letter.

options.text: Please let me know if any further information is required.
options.feedback: This anticipates the reader's needs politely and is a normal part of a formal closing.

options.text: I look forward to hearing from you at your earliest convenience.
options.feedback: This is the conventional formal expression of an expected reply.

questions.explanation:
A short formal letter needs a clear purpose, an offer of further help and a courteous expectation of a reply, and none of these involves fillers or a dismissive tone.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which paragraph belongs in the well-written email rather than the poor one?
questions.context: A teacher is comparing a well-written formal email with a poorly written one about the same request.

options.text: I am writing to request a change of lab room for Thursday, since our current room seats only eighteen of our twenty-four students.
options.feedback: Correct. It names the purpose, gives a specific verifiable reason with figures and makes the request in a single courteous sentence.

options.text: Hi, the room is too small, it is a fact, and we need a change, so fix it, thanks.
options.feedback: The casual opening and the bare imperative replace the formal request with a demand.

options.text: Rooms, seats, students, numbers: these are the things that matter in this kind of letter.
options.feedback: Listing the nouns states the topic without making any request, so the reader has no action to take.

options.text: It is not possible to say that the room is small, although everyone knows it is.
options.feedback: The sentence denies a claim nobody made and concedes one nobody disputed, so it says nothing about the request.

questions.explanation:
A well-written formal email states the purpose, gives a specific verifiable reason and makes one courteous request; poor ones rely on tone, lists of nouns or self-contradiction.
---
questions.subject: ingles
